title: The hidden generational economy links paid production, public transfers, unpaid care, and fiscal sustainability across the life course
source_unit: UN DESA Population Division, Policy Brief No. 187: Revealing the Generational Economy: An Essential System at Risk
geography: Global demographic and social systems, with examples and methodological applications spanning low-, middle-, and high-income countries

denominator.unit: society-wide life-course system of intergenerational production, consumption, sharing, and allocation

flow_set.value: monetary transfers, time transfers, caregiving, domestic services, public programs, taxes, savings, production, and consumption

life_course_roles.value: people move between receiving and providing support over the life course

gdp_boundary.value: conventional economic measures such as GDP do not fully capture the resource flows connecting generations

observations.method: UN DESA policy synthesis defining the generational economy through social institutions, markets, public institutions, monetary flows, time transfers, and life-course roles.
observations.uncertainty: The framework identifies resources and relationships that standard accounts omit or separate; it does not assign a single monetary value or causal effect to every family, public, or market transfer.
observations.subgroup: Children, working-age adults, older persons, caregivers, families, employers, public institutions, and people moving between support-provider and support-recipient roles.
observations.counterinterpretation: GDP and national accounts remain essential for many macroeconomic purposes; complementary generational accounts deepen rather than replace existing economic measurement.

denominator.unit: countries experiencing changing fertility, working-age populations, or population ageing

younger_country_opportunity.value: declining fertility and expanding working-age populations can create a demographic dividend if human-capital investment and employment are sufficient

ageing_pressure.value: rising shares of older persons increase demand for health and long-term care and pressure pension and public-finance systems

ageing_before_rich.value: many countries face the prospect of growing old before growing rich

equity_questions.value: fiscal sustainability, intergenerational equity, inclusive growth, and social cohesion

observations.method: UN DESA synthesis of demographic transition, population ageing, public finance, care demand, human-capital investment, and intergenerational resource flows.
observations.uncertainty: Demographic structure changes gradually but its economic effects depend on employment, migration, health, productivity, policy design, and family and community institutions.
observations.subgroup: Young and older populations, working-age contributors, caregivers, pensioners, health and long-term-care users, and countries with different fiscal and demographic capacities.
observations.counterinterpretation: Ageing can coincide with longer healthy lives, continued work, productivity, and social contribution; a demographic dividend is possible but never automatic.

observations.period: 2026; accounting tools and national statistical capacity

denominator.unit: national accounting and population-statistics systems covered by UN DESA methodology

accounting_frameworks.value: National Transfer Accounts, National Time Transfer Accounts, and National Inclusion Accounts

nta_scope.value: production, consumption, asset income, and transfers by age group

ntta_scope.value: unpaid caregiving and domestic services within households

ntai_scope.value: economic flows disaggregated by age and socioeconomic status

observations.method: UN DESA methodological description of NTA, NTTA, and NTA-I/National Inclusion Accounts as complementary extensions to national accounting.
observations.uncertainty: Accounting frameworks improve visibility but depend on survey, administrative, time-use, income, expenditure, and demographic data quality; estimates are not direct observation of every transfer.
observations.subgroup: National statistical offices, fiscal planners, care systems, households, unpaid caregivers, public programs, and social groups distributed across age and socioeconomic status.
observations.counterinterpretation: Disaggregated accounts can reveal patterns without resolving normative choices about redistribution, and they should be interpreted with qualitative, institutional, and rights-based evidence.

denominator.unit: public budget, social-protection, care, health, education, and development-planning systems

planning_use.value: integrated accounts can support inclusive and sustainable fiscal-budget planning under population ageing

life_course_finance.value: education, health, income security, pensions, and care allocate resources across the life course

future_orientation.value: long-term and intergenerational perspectives should be embedded in decision-making

social_cohesion_link.value: how societies distribute resources and risks across generations affects inequality reduction and social cohesion

observations.method: UN DESA policy brief linking generational accounting to fiscal planning, social protection, care, public services, inclusive growth, and intergenerational decision-making.
observations.uncertainty: Better measurement does not guarantee politically feasible or equitable policy; implementation depends on institutions, budgets, gender relations, labor markets, and public choices.
observations.subgroup: Public finance ministries, social-protection and care systems, families, workers, older persons, children, women performing unpaid care, and future generations.
observations.counterinterpretation: Intergenerational framing should not pit age groups against one another: people can be both contributors and recipients, and universal systems may create reciprocal benefits across the life course.

related_sources.claim: UN DESA National Inclusion Accounts Manual extends generational accounting to age and socioeconomic-status differences.
UN DESA National Transfer Accounts page describes NTA, NTTA, and National Inclusion Accounts and their policy use.
UN DESA publication index provides the 2026 policy-brief framing for generational economy and ageing.

boundary: This record adds a generational-economy and measurement-capacity route linking paid production, public transfers, unpaid care, age structure, fiscal planning, and intergenerational equity. It is not a respondent-level time-use analysis, an individual care trajectory, a forecast of fiscal solvency, or proof that one age group causes another group’s outcomes.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official UN DESA policy brief, National Transfer Accounts page, publication index, and National Inclusion Accounts Manual page were reviewed; generational-flow, demographic-strain, accounting-framework, and planning claims were cross-checked.
